analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurance plans to cover fertility treatment, including IVF, with no extra cost-sharing.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 6 Democratic cosponsors, has sat in the Senate Health Committee since July 2025 with no committee vote or floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require group and individual health insurance plans that cover pregnancy care to also cover fertility treatment — including freezing eggs or embryos, insemination, in vitro fertilization, embryo testing, and fertility medications. Patients could not be charged higher deductibles or coinsurance for fertility care than for other medical services, and insurers could not pressure patients or doctors away from it. The same rules would extend to federal employees' plans, military families (TRICARE), veterans and their spouses, Medicaid, and Medicare.
analysis.who_benefits: People who need fertility care to have a child — including those diagnosed with infertility and those who need to preserve fertility before cancer treatment or other medical care. Today a single IVF cycle commonly costs $15,000-$30,000 out of pocket, which puts treatment out of reach for most middle-income families. The bill would make coverage available regardless of an infertility diagnosis, cap cost-sharing at what plans charge for other care, and extend coverage to veterans, military families, federal employees, Medicaid enrollees, and Medicare beneficiaries.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People paying out of pocket for IVF

how_it_helps.text: Requires any health plan that covers obstetrical services to cover fertility treatment — egg/sperm/embryo preservation, artificial insemination, IVF, embryo genetic testing, fertility medications, and gamete donation — whether or not the patient has an infertility diagnosis [S2].
Bars plans from imposing deductibles or coinsurance on fertility treatment that exceed what they charge for other medical services [S2].
Prohibits insurers from offering incentives to skip treatment, penalizing providers who give it, or discriminating against patients under existing civil rights laws [S2].

Extends the same coverage to federal employee health plans, TRICARE for military families, veterans and their spouses or partners, Medicaid, and Medicare, with Medicare waiving the deductible and paying 100% of the approved charge for fertility treatment [S2].
Plans may not refuse to cover a patient just because they haven't been diagnosed as infertile under the standard medical definition, if a provider deems the treatment appropriate [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurance plans and the employers and consumers who fund them bear the added cost of covering fertility treatment. Because a IVF cycle costs far more than typical care, spreading that cost across all enrollees would likely raise premiums somewhat, including for people who never use fertility services. Federal taxpayers fund the added coverage in Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE, and veterans' care.

drawbacks.text: A broad coverage mandate raises premiums for everyone in the plan, including people who will never need fertility care; IVF is among the most expensive per-patient benefits, so the premium effect would be real and spread widely [S2].

The bill requires coverage regardless of an infertility diagnosis, which is broader than most state fertility mandates; critics of that approach argue it expands covered use and cost beyond medically diagnosed need [S2].

The bill does not provide new funding to offset insurers' costs, so the mandate works entirely through higher premiums and higher federal payments in Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE, and veterans' programs [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly one in several couples who experience infertility, the benefit is large — coverage that turns a five-figure out-of-pocket bill into a routine insurance claim. The cost is spread thin across everyone with insurance through modestly higher premiums and some added federal spending. The tradeoff is genuine but lopsided toward patients; the main honest objection is that a mandate is a hidden premium increase rather than a funded benefit, and the no-infertility-diagnosis requirement makes it broader than most existing state mandates.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in July 2025 and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it has remained without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the Access to Fertility Treatment and Care Act on July 23, 2025, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S4].
Six senators, all Democrats, cosponsored the bill [S3].
No further action — no committee vote, hearing, or floor consideration — appears in the bill's action history since referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers are better off so far: with no committee or floor action, no coverage mandate has taken effect, and premiums need not rise. Families paying five-figure IVF bills remain uncovered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers, for now — no mandate has taken effect

sides.party_line_note: All six cosponsors are Democrats, and the bill sits in a Senate committee controlled by Republicans, who have not scheduled action on it.

industries.note: The bill requires plans that cover pregnancy care to also cover fertility treatment — including IVF — without extra cost-sharing, adding a high-cost benefit insurers must fund through premiums. Insurers benefit from the mandate not taking effect.

Mandated coverage with cost-sharing caps would make IVF and related services affordable to many more patients, expanding the pool of people who can pay for treatment. Providers also gain protection from reimbursement penalties under the bill.
The bill requires coverage of fertility medications, including over-the-counter drugs indicated for fertility, creating a larger insured market for these drugs.
Employers who fund group coverage would absorb part of the added cost of the mandate. Some large employers already offer IVF benefits voluntarily, so the effect is uneven across employers.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has no Republican cosponsors and sits in a Republican-controlled committee with no scheduled action. Standalone coverage mandates rarely reach the Senate floor on their own; the realistic path to a vote would be attachment to a larger health package, which has not been indicated. Expect the bill to remain in committee unless fertility coverage becomes part of a broader deal.
